analysis.one_liner: Lets Puerto Rico and other U.S. territories wipe out unsecured debts and audits how that debt was built.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2019, sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let Puerto Rico and other U.S. territories cancel their public unsecured debts if they meet hardship tests, such as a shrinking population, a recent major disaster, or heavy per-person debt. To soften the blow, it creates a $15 billion federal fund that compensates smaller creditors, including ordinary individual bondholders and local banks, while shutting out hedge funds and big financial institutions. It also creates an independent commission to audit every Puerto Rico public debt issued since 1972 and publish the findings.
analysis.who_benefits: The more than three million U.S. citizens of Puerto Rico and residents of other territories, who otherwise repay unsupported debt through higher taxes and cuts to schools, hospitals, and services. Also retirees and public workers, because pensions, vendor bills, and tax refunds are protected from discharge, and small creditors who are compensated: individual investors who held bonds before Hurricane María, local banks and credit unions, Puerto Rico pension plans, and small open-end mutual funds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Puerto Rico residents and small local creditors

how_it_helps.text: A territory can discharge its unsecured public debt by a simple vote of its own legislature if it meets two of three hardship tests: population down more than 5% over ten years, receipt of major federal disaster assistance within five years, or per capita debt above $15,000.
The discharge protects public employee pensions, health benefits, payments owed to vendors and service providers, and pending tax refunds, which cannot be canceled.

A $15 billion compensation fund, split evenly between creditors living in Puerto Rico and those outside it, pays eligible claimants for their losses, prioritizing individuals who held their bonds before Hurricane María (September 20, 2017), local banks, credit unions, businesses, pension plans, worker associations, and open-end mutual funds that waive management fees.

Hedge funds, unregistered investment companies, financial guaranty insurers, parties to swaps and repurchase agreements, and any financial institution with more than $2 billion in assets are barred from the compensation fund.

An independent Puerto Rico Public Credit Comprehensive Audit Commission must review all public debt issued since fiscal year 1972, publish a public database, and can recommend administrative, civil, or criminal action over how the debt was contracted.

analysis.who_pays: Bondholders whose unsecured Puerto Rico debt is wiped out, particularly hedge funds and large financial institutions that receive no compensation, plus federal taxpayers, since the $15 billion compensation fund is appropriated from the Treasury as emergency spending added to the deficit. Territories that use the discharge would also likely face higher borrowing costs afterward.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $15 billion from the Treasury, designated as emergency spending that is not offset, adding to the deficit; unobligated funds are returned only after 36 months.

Large bondholders, bond insurers, and institutions above $2 billion in assets lose their entire unsecured claim with no compensation, and markets for territorial debt would likely demand higher interest rates afterward, raising future borrowing costs for the very residents the bill helps.

The discharge overrides contractual promises and the bill tries to block Fifth Amendment takings challenges through exclusive local-court jurisdiction and estoppel rules, an aggressive use of federal power that courts could have partially struck down.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Puerto Rico's 3.2 million U.S. citizens, who were already living through bankruptcy, a decade of population loss, Hurricane María, and federal austerity, the gain would have been large: no longer servicing debt that, as the bill's own findings state, 'cannot realistically be repaid without imposing undue hardship.' The costs are real but narrower: losses fall on bondholders who knowingly bought risky territory debt, including hedge funds that bought deeply discounted paper expecting full repayment, and taxpayers fund $15 billion in compensation, though much of that money flows to ordinary individual investors and local banks rather than Wall Street. The audit commission adds accountability for how decades of debt were incurred. The main design risk is legal fragility and a lasting borrowing penalty for territories that use the discharge.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the United States Territorial Relief Act of 2019 on May 2, 2019, joined by Senators Sanders, Harris, Markey, and Gillibrand.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote, and the bill expired with the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

All five original supporters were Democrats plus one Independent (Sanders); no Republican ever cosponsored the bill, and Republicans controlled the Senate and its committee schedule during this period.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Holders of Puerto Rico debt came out ahead: the PROMESA court restructuring continued under existing rules, and hedge funds, bond insurers, and large institutions that would have seen unsecured claims discharged, and been barred from the compensation fund, kept their full recovery paths instead. The audit commission that could have exposed how the debt was built was never created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Puerto Rico bondholders and large financial institutions

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited four colleagues as original cosponsors.

for.name: Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Kamala Harris (D-CA), Edward Markey (D-MA), and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, its only congressional support.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill in the entire 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Senate took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and large financial institutions holding Puerto Rico debt
industries.note: Their unsecured claims would be discharged outright and they are expressly barred from the $15 billion compensation fund (any institution over $2 billion in assets is excluded). Their gain from the bill failing was keeping full recovery rights against Puerto Rico at the expense of its residents.

Bond insurers that paid out on Puerto Rico defaults are defined in the bill, denied compensation fund eligibility, and lose the underlying claims they indemnified. Their interest in avoiding the discharge ran against debt relief for island residents.

industries.industry: Local Puerto Rico banks, credit unions, and small businesses that bought territory debt
industries.note: They would lose their unsecured claims like everyone else but are first in line for compensation from the federal fund, giving them a federal backstop rather than years of litigation.

Open-end mutual funds lose their claims to discharge but can claim compensation if their managers waive fees on the payout, so they are partially protected; closed-end funds and unregistered investment vehicles are excluded entirely.

industries.industry: Puerto Rico public employee pension plans
industries.note: Pensions and retiree health benefits are carved out of the discharge and must be repaid in full, and pension plans are also eligible claimants for the compensation fund.
